{
  "strategy": "increase_dram_bw_to_128",
  "hardware_update": {
    "num_chiplets": 32,
    "compute_units": 16384,
    "buffer_size": 8192,
    "system_params": {"dram_bw": 128, "nop_bw": 128, "micro_batch": 2, "tensor_parall": 32},
    "chiplet_type": "ws"
  },
  "selected_hardware_candidate": "modify_hardware_parameter_610a634ba8b055a6",
  "actions": ["dram_bw: 64->128"],
  "rationale": "Current best (iteration 3, objective 8.49e26) has 32 WS chiplets at max compute_units (16384). The bottleneck is mixed: FFN1 compute-bound layers (68.4% of time, 99.9% calc, already at max CU) and critical-path tail layers (norm2, res2, GeLU, res1) that are 50-59% memory-bound and 40-56% communication-bound. Core utilization is only 45.5%, with the critical path ending at 10.58s on core5 via norm2 (57.4% memory time, 42.3% communication). Increasing DRAM BW from 64 to 128 directly reduces the memory component of these critical-path tail layers, lowering the critical end time and reducing memory energy. IO cost is only 7.9% of total MC ($35.27), so doubling DRAM BW has a modest MC impact. This is a cost-effective targeted move compared to increasing chiplet count (which would increase OS cost at 39.4% of MC) or NoP BW (which historically failed on 16 chiplets with 73% objective worsening due to MC doubling).",
  "notes": {
    "history_usage": "Retrieved case (score 0.8895) showed NoP BW 128->256 on 16 chiplets worsened objective by 73% due to MC doubling from $237.6 to $418.3. This negative evidence supports avoiding another NoP increase. Retrieved case (score 0.8455) showed num_chiplets 16->32 with tp=32 improved objective by 12%, but that move has already been applied. The current hardware already has 32 chiplets at max CU, so further chiplet increases would face diminishing returns with low core utilization (45.5%). The DRAM BW increase is a new direction not yet explored in the trajectory.",
    "cost_risk": "Monetary cost expected to increase modestly. IO cost is only 7.9% of total MC ($35.27). Doubling DRAM BW from 64 to 128 should increase IO cost by roughly 2x, adding ~$35 to total MC (~$448), a ~8% increase. This is acceptable because the latency reduction from faster DRAM access on critical-path tail layers (norm2, res2, GeLU, res1) and potential energy reduction should compensate.",
    "expected_objective_direction": "decrease",
    "rejected_alternatives": [
      "NoP BW 128->256: rejected because historical case on 16 chiplets caused 73% objective worsening; on 32 chiplets the IO cost share is still small but the critical-path layers have more DRAM time than NoC time, making DRAM BW the more impactful constraint.",
      "num_chiplets 32->64: rejected because core utilization is only 45.5%, indicating many cores are already idle; doubling chiplet count would increase OS cost (39.4% of MC) significantly without clear latency benefit.",
      "buffer_size 8192->32768: rejected because buffer is not a bottleneck (0% buffer time in root cause summary); increasing buffer would add cost without addressing the memory/communication critical-path tail.",
      "micro_batch 2->4: rejected because the compute-bound FFN1 layers already dominate latency; increasing micro_batch would increase compute load without addressing the critical-path tail."
    ],
    "risk": "Main risk: the critical-path tail layers have both memory (50-59%) and communication (40-56%) components. DRAM BW increase only addresses the memory component, not the communication component. If the communication component dominates after DRAM improvement, the latency reduction may be smaller than expected. Additionally, the compute-bound FFN1 layers (68.4% of time) are unaffected by DRAM BW, limiting total latency improvement. However, the low cost and targeted nature of this move make it a low-risk exploration."
  }
}
